actions.justification: MANDATORY: Assess mental status immediately in DKA to evaluate severity and guide airway management decisions. Altered mental status indicates severe DKA requiring more aggressive management.

MANDATORY: BMP is critical to check serum potassium BEFORE initiating insulin. Per ADA guidelines, insulin must be withheld if K+ < 3.3 mEq/L to prevent life-threatening hypokalemia. Also assesses renal function and baseline electrolytes.
MANDATORY: Point-of-care glucose establishes baseline and guides fluid and insulin management. Glucose monitoring every 1-2 hours is required per DKA protocol.
MANDATORY action - must confirm ketosis to support DKA diagnosis and assess severity. Required within 60-minute deadline.

Per ADA DKA guidelines, IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline (1-1.5 L/hr) should begin within 15 minutes of presentation. Patient has tachycardia (HR 105) and vomiting indicating dehydration. This is the cornerstone of DKA management and must precede insulin.

Blood gas is essential to quantify pH and bicarbonate to confirm DKA severity classification, guide bicarbonate therapy decisions, and monitor treatment response. RR of 24 suggests compensatory Kussmaul breathing.

ADA DKA guidelines require potassium replacement if K+ < 5.3 mEq/L before starting insulin. DKA causes total body potassium depletion, and insulin will drive K+ intracellularly, risking life-threatening hypokalemia. Replacement should be initiated while monitoring levels.
ADA guidelines require glucose monitoring every 1 hour during DKA management to guide fluid and insulin therapy adjustments and detect hypoglycemia.
Anion gap is a key marker of DKA severity and resolution. Monitoring anion gap helps confirm closure of the gap as a criterion for DKA resolution alongside pH normalization and bicarbonate recovery.

Potassium replacement has been given and labs are pending. Must confirm K+ > 3.3 mEq/L before starting insulin, and K+ < 5.3 mEq/L to continue replacement. Serial potassium monitoring is critical in DKA management to prevent life-threatening hypokalemia when insulin is initiated.
Reassessing the anion gap helps track DKA resolution. Anion gap closure is a key endpoint of treatment, and trending this value guides ongoing management of fluid resuscitation and insulin therapy.

Once K+ is confirmed > 3.3 mEq/L (potassium replacement given, monitoring in progress), regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr should be initiated per ADA DKA protocol to correct hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis. This is the next critical step after electrolyte stabilization.

Patient has ongoing DKA with moderate severity; reassessing hydration status guides continued fluid resuscitation needs and monitors response to initial NS bolus given the tachycardia (HR 105) and clinical picture.

Although pH is pending, patient has RR 24 suggesting significant acidosis; bicarbonate may be indicated if pH < 6.9 per ADA guidelines. Checking eligibility now ensures no delay if severe acidosis is confirmed.
Mandatory action: patient has tachycardia (HR 105) and elevated RR (24), needs vital sign reassessment to monitor response to fluid resuscitation and detect hemodynamic deterioration.
Mandatory action: IV access is required for fluid resuscitation and all IV medications in DKA management.
Mandatory action: ABG is needed to monitor pH and bicarbonate to classify DKA severity and guide management, especially since blood gas results are still pending.

MANDATORY action - Normal saline IV fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of DKA management. While a fluid bolus was given, continuous NS infusion must be formally started to maintain adequate hydration and correct the hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state.
Calculating the anion gap is essential to confirm DKA diagnosis and establish a baseline for monitoring resolution. Anion gap closure is a key endpoint for DKA treatment.

Assessing anion gap closure helps determine if DKA is resolving. Resolution criteria include anion gap normalization, pH >7.3, and bicarbonate >18 mEq/L. This guides decisions about transitioning from IV to subcutaneous insulin.
Labs have been ordered and fluid resuscitation initiated. Now classify DKA severity based on pH, bicarbonate, and anion gap results to guide ongoing management intensity and disposition decisions.
With hyperglycemia in DKA, corrected sodium calculation is needed to assess true sodium status and guide fluid management.
Moderate DKA with vomiting, tachycardia, and tachypnea warrants ICU admission for close monitoring of fluid balance, electrolytes, glucose, and insulin infusion titration per ADA guidelines.
